planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in fall or early spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil along shaded streambanks or seepage areas; give this the largest footprint of any western shade perennial, 6-8 feet in every direction.

directions: Site in reliably moist to wet, humus-rich soil along the shaded margins of streams, seeps, or canyon bottoms in part shade; unlike its eastern relative American spikenard, this West Coast native from the redwood and mixed-evergreen forests of California and southern Oregon demands consistent moisture and will scorch or stall in dry shade. Huge doubly compound leaves on stout, unarmed stems can reach 3-5 feet long, giving a coarse, almost gunnera-like presence at the back of a moist woodland border. Rounded clusters of small greenish-white flowers open in summer, followed by dark purple-black berries favored by birds and once eaten by several Native American groups along with the aromatic roots. Herbaceous top growth dies back hard with the first frosts and re-emerges vigorously from a stout woody crown each spring, so mark its location and mulch generously over winter.
sources: Las Pilitas Nursery native plant database
